newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa political violence drops sharply - report.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa political violence drops sharply - report.

text.p: Political violence in South Africa has plummeted to a quarter of the peak rate recorded in 1993, the country's independent Human Rights Commission said in a report published on Monday.
The HRC was set up in 1988 to monitor violence and human rights in the struggle over apartheid.

It said in its annual report for 1996 that it had identified many positive signs three years after the first all-race elections brought President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress to power in 1994.
"Paramount is the decline in political violence for the third consecutive year to the lowest total recorded in our existence," the HRC said.
The commission said 1,057 people died in all forms of political violence in 1996, down from 1,296 in 1995 and from a peak of 4,406 in 1993.

It said in a separate monthly report for May that although 340 people died in all forms of political violence in the first five months of this year, the monthly average for 1997 was down to 68 from 81.5 in 1996.
The monthly report added that taxi violence, in which passengers are targeted by hitmen acting for rival taxi operators, remained a key concern.

The annual report said positive signs "need to be weighed against the still substantial numbers of people dying in political violence, the terrible carnage as a result of taxi violence (and) continuing tensions on the nation's campuses."
It added: "A central feature which emerges from our monitoring of political violence around the country...is the desperate state of the country's criminal justice system."
Police and courts are strained by a big rise in non-political crime and violence since apartheid was lifted.
Businesses cite crime, ranging from rape and murder to hijacking of cars and trucks, as the major impediment to investment and to South Africa's bid to host the Olympic Games in 2004.
The HRC, a target of government harassment before the dismantling of apartheid, was critical of aspects of the new government's record.
Citing continued imprisonment of juveniles and a perceived slowing of the commitment to international human rights accords, the HRC said:
"Government's response to specific issues which arose during the year raises concern...The measures have been ad hoc, reactive and, at times, to the detriment of human rights."
It called for urgent attention to the carnage in the battle for the country's most lucrative taxi routes out of black townships.

"Perhaps the Achilles heel of South Africa in 1996 has been taxi violence. We record a huge upsurge in this violence from 202 deaths in 1995 to 322 deaths in 1996, with this violence affecting most provinces," the commission said.
